Recent evidence supports treating sampled-candidate diagnostics cautiously. RecSys 2025’s [On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) separates model separability, agreement with full evaluation, robustness to exposure bias, and alignment with true preferences; negative-sampling choices affect these dimensions. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds aggregate metrics hide substantial head/mid/tail differences. Neither establishes that a particular diagnostic predicts failures for this HSTU benchmark.

Practical inference: prioritize target rank, negative-outranking fraction, and the target’s position relative to the top-10 boundary. These survive strictly increasing score transformations with consistent tie handling. Raw logit margins do not; dividing the target-minus-boundary margin by within-user score standard deviation gives positive-affine invariance, but not general monotonic invariance. Report HR@10 by training-history length and training-item-frequency bands, with eligible-user counts and slice denominators. Recommendation exposure can be normalized by catalog share or training-frequency share, but these are descriptive reference distributions—not measured exposure propensities. Interaction-only data cannot identify actual exposure or justify causal exposure correction.

For one trained HSTU model/category, keep the host’s fixed 99-negative HR@10 and four-category macro average as the selection criterion. Proposed supplementary checks: paired user-level bootstrap intervals, resampling within categories before macro averaging; and exact full-catalog ranking on a small, fixed validation-user subset, scoring items in chunks and preserving eligibility rules. Compare sampled/full-catalog hit disagreement and target ranks on those same users. This bounds audit cost while testing sampling artifacts; it does not estimate full-catalog accuracy for every user or replace the host evaluator.
